solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Animal trapping bug rolled in syrup

indicators.note: the animal word holds the next piece within it, as a trap holds its catch

parts.note: a pig is a farm animal

indicators.note: rolled over, so the word for bug is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a wire is a hidden listening device, a bug

explanation.surface: A creature has a bug stuck to it after rolling in sticky syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'syrup' looks like the sticky stuff, but it is Cockney rhyming slang: syrup of figs = wig. 'rolled' makes ERIW.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang, syrup of figs, makes syrup a wig, and a periwig is an old-fashioned powdered wig.

clue.text: 'The Lady's not for Burning', one's opening shows?

definitions.text: 'The Lady's not for Burning', one's opening shows?

parts.words: 'The Lady's not for Burning', one's opening shows
parts.note: when this sunshade is opened, it shows that the lady will not get sunburnt

explanation.surface: A theatre programme notes the opening of the Christopher Fry play The Lady's Not for Burning.
explanation.walkthrough: The Christopher Fry play title is a red herring: 'opening' is unfurling an umbrella, not a first night.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasol is a light umbrella carried to shade a lady from the sun.

clue.text: Avian pet, upset without a perch, sounded out

indicators.note: without means the a is removed from the reversed pet word
upset in a down clue means the pet word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: dear is a term of endearment, a pet

indicators.note: sounded out means the word for perch is heard, not seen

parts.note: a perch, rod or pole is an old measure of length, five and a half yards

explanation.surface: A pet bird is upset because it has no perch and makes a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns DEAR into RAED; 'without a' drops its A to give RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Avian means a bird, used as a noun, and the redpoll is a small finch.

clue.text: Hit with right going in for hard torture

indicators.note: the right letter goes in to take the hard letter's place

parts.note: to whack is to hit hard
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A beating with the right hand, the start of severe torture.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrack is a variant of rack, the torture device that stretches the victim, and the verb to torment.

clue.text: Snail and rabbit, too French, bizarre almost

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for to chatter, and so is to gas
trop is French for too

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the bizarre word is dropped

parts.note: odd means bizarre

explanation.surface: A snail and a rabbit, in too French and odd a combination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit' is a verb here, British slang for talking on and on (rabbit and pork = talk).
explanation.definitionFit: A snail is a mollusc of the class Gastropoda, so it is an example of the class.

clue.text: Sidelines half of side caught by protests

indicators.note: the protests word catches the next piece and holds it inside

parts.note: demos are protest marches

indicators.note: only the first two of the four letters of the side word are used

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A manager benches half the team while protesters gather outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' keeps the first two letters of the four-letter word for side.
explanation.definitionFit: To sideline someone is to push them aside into a lesser role, which is a demotion.

clue.text: Drops tend oddly to get prescribed

indicators.note: oddly means the first, third, fifth and every other odd-placed letter is taken

explanation.surface: A nurse tends to give eye drops in odd amounts as prescribed.
explanation.definitionFit: A patient who has been dosed has been given the prescribed amount of medicine.

clue.text: Grimace, eating small slice — flipping cheese!

indicators.note: the grimace word eats the small letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a moue is a pout, a grimace

indicators.note: flipping turns the slice word over, so it is read backwards

parts.note: a part is a portion, a slice

explanation.surface: Someone pulls a face over a thin slice of cheese and exclaims 'flipping cheese!'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British oath; here it turns PART into TRAP. Mousetrap is British slang for cheap, ordinary cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is British slang for poor, bland cheese, the kind fit only to bait traps.

clue.text: Leaves for a calming break?

parts.note: dried leaves smoked for relaxation during a cigarette break

explanation.surface: Someone goes off for a restful break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb (departs) but is the noun: plant leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco is the cured leaves of a plant, smoked to calm the nerves.

clue.text: Eat noisily, left to finish American excess

indicators.note: the left letter goes to the finish, moving to the end of the word

parts.note: to slurp is to eat or drink noisily

explanation.surface: An American eats noisily and leaves their food to finish later: excess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left to finish' moves the L of SLURP to the end, giving SURPL.
explanation.definitionFit: A surplus is an amount beyond what is needed, an excess.

clue.text: Return of Queen creates art in charts again

indicators.note: a return sends the Queen's abbreviation back the other way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
someone who draws creates art

explanation.surface: A monarch's homecoming prompts artists to sketch new charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return of' turns ER into RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To redraw is to draw again, as a mapmaker redoes a chart or a boundary.

clue.text: Start to saw logs?

indicators.note: the first letter of the saw word is taken, its start

parts.note: lumber is cut timber, logs

explanation.surface: A woodsman about to begin cutting up logs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw logs' is an idiom for snoring, so the whole clue also describes falling asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To start sawing logs is to start snoring, which is dropping into sleep.

clue.text: Blocked by colour after swerve ends round hole

indicators.note: the colour word comes after the rest
the end letters of the swerve word go round the hole word, enclosing it
the first and last letters of the swerve word are its ends

parts.note: a nook is a recess or small hole
red is a colour

explanation.surface: A snooker shot: blocked by a coloured ball after swerving round a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a snooker table, with swerve and hole as shot and pocket; the answer is itself the snooker term.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker a player left with no clear shot at a ball is said to be blocked off in this way, hence thwarted generally.

clue.text: Better English law's overturned, Conservative's admitted

indicators.note: the law piece lets the Conservative letter in, admitting it inside
overturned means the Latin word for law is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: A Conservative government overturns an English law in the name of improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' makes XEL from LEX; C is admitted after its X.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to outdo or surpass, so it works as the verb better.

clue.text: Tree ring circling heart of fir all over

indicators.note: the whole construction is turned over, reading backwards
the ring word circles the central letter, holding it inside

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them on the phone

indicators.note: the middle letter of the fir word is its heart

explanation.surface: A ring of trees circles a fir that is right at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: CALL round I gives CALIL, and 'all over' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: The lilac is a small flowering tree or shrub, with scented purple or white blossom.

clue.text: Removal of mad King in endless abandon

indicators.note: the king's name sits inside the shortened abandon word
endless means the last letter of the abandon word is dropped

parts.note: to cancel a plan is to abandon it
King Lear, in Shakespeare, goes mad

explanation.surface: A mad king being removed from power with wild abandon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandon' looks like a noun (wildness) but is a verb, cancel.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearance is the act of clearing away, a removal, as in slum clearance.

clue.text: Bust out of prison facing questioning, not caught

indicators.note: the prison word stands in front of the next piece

parts.note: pen is slang for a prison, short for penitentiary

indicators.note: not means the caught letter is left out of the questioning word

parts.note: curious means inquisitive, questioning
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A convict breaks out of jail ahead of police questioning, and is not caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' is the adjective meaning broke, not a breakout.
explanation.definitionFit: Bust as in broke means penniless, and penurious means extremely poor.

clue.text: Possibly worms pet coming up in lumps

indicators.note: the reversed pet word sits inside the lumps word

parts.note: nodes are knobs or lumps

indicators.note: coming up in a down clue means the pet word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a tame animal is a pet

explanation.surface: A pet with lumps that might be worms coming up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns TAME into EMAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Nematodes are roundworms, and 'possibly' marks worms as a wider class that includes them.

clue.text: Port and crackers passed left by so-and-so

indicators.note: the crackers piece goes next to the so-and-so word

parts.note: a rotter is a cad, a so-and-so

indicators.note: passed to the left, so the crackers word runs right to left, backwards

parts.note: crackers means mad

explanation.surface: At dinner, port and crackers are passed along the table by some rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: Port is passed to the left at table; here 'passed left' turns MAD into DAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam in the Netherlands is one of the world's biggest seaports.

clue.text: Original artist bedridden, possibly catching cold

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

indicators.note: the bedridden piece catches the cold letter, holding it inside

parts.note: bedridden is laid up; read as LAID turned up, it gives this word

explanation.surface: An original artist is laid up in bed and may have caught a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedridden is 'laid up'; read as an instruction in a down clue, 'up' turns LAID into DIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical can mean fresh and new, completely departing from what went before, so original.

clue.text: Puppet bird replacing 'American Dad!' in household

indicators.note: the bird word replaces the American father word in the household word

parts.note: a household name is a popular one
pop is an American word for a father
a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: A puppet bird replaces the cartoon American Dad in a household's viewing.
explanation.definitionFit: A puppet ruler is a titular one: holding a title without real power.

clue.text: Dish done by middle Italy

indicators.note: the middle letter goes next to the done word

parts.note: something done is over, past

indicators.note: the central letter of the five-letter Italy word

explanation.surface: A recipe finished off in central Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is a staple Italian food served as a dish such as spaghetti or lasagne.

clue.text: Turn restricting learner following Scrabble's opening tile

indicators.note: the turn piece follows the Scrabble letter
the first letter of the Scrabble word opens it
the turn word restricts the learner letter, holding it inside

parts.note: to hinge is to turn on a pivot
L is the learner driver abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Scrabble learner's turn, restricted to playing the opening tile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tile' is not a Scrabble tile but a roofing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle is a thin wooden roofing tile.

clue.text: Helped President Kennedy to hold seat finally

indicators.note: the president and Kennedy names together hold the next letter inside

parts.note: Abe Lincoln was a US President
Ted Kennedy was a US senator

indicators.note: the last letter of the seat word

explanation.surface: A President Kennedy finally takes hold of a seat with help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'President Kennedy' reads as one man, JFK, but it is two: Lincoln and Ted Kennedy.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to aid or assist, usually in wrongdoing, so abetted means helped.

clue.text: Bambi running across Thumper's first put off

indicators.note: the Bambi word runs across, straddling the next letter

parts.note: Bambi, the Disney fawn, is a deer

indicators.note: only the first letter of the Thumper word is taken

explanation.surface: A Disney scene: Bambi runs across, put off by his rabbit friend Thumper.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter someone is to discourage them, to put them off doing something.

clue.text: Holmes, perhaps imperfect, having time for female

indicators.note: having time for female means the time letter takes the female letter's place

parts.note: defective means faulty, imperfect

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes is flawed, finding time for women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' just links: the word for imperfect has its F swapped for a T.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is the most famous fictional sleuth, an example of an investigator, flagged by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: 'Carry on Dick' initially with team up

indicators.note: the first letter goes with the team up word
the first letter of the Dick word is taken

parts.note: to ally is to team up

explanation.surface: The Carry On film Carry On Dick, with its team of actors starting up.
explanation.walkthrough: Carry On films are a long-running British comedy series; Carry On Dick (1974) is one. Here 'carry on' means flirt.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on with someone is to flirt or have an affair, and to dally is to trifle amorously.

clue.text: Dresses boy in free clothes

indicators.note: the boy word sits in the cut-down clothes word
free means the clothes word is freed of its inner letters, leaving its ends

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Someone dresses a boy in clothes that cost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' looks like 'free of charge'; it removes LOTHE from 'clothes', leaving CS.
explanation.definitionFit: To clad is to clothe or cover, so clads means dresses.

clue.text: Officer's some guts approaching centre of enemy line

indicators.note: the guts word comes up next to the following piece

parts.note: the colon is part of the intestines, some of the guts

indicators.note: the middle letter of the five-letter enemy word

explanation.surface: An officer's courage as he nears the middle of the enemy line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guts' looks like courage, but it means intestines here.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonel is a senior army officer, ranking above a lieutenant colonel.

clue.text: Swallow medicine taking a shot off and on

indicators.note: the medicine word takes in the a, holding it inside

parts.note: a drug is a medicine

indicators.note: letters of the shot word are skipped and taken in turn, the second and fourth

explanation.surface: Someone gulps medicine and has an injection now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off and on' takes the even letters H and T of 'shot'.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught is a single gulp or swallow of drink, as in drinking in one draught.

clue.text: Crime of non-clergy holding service around church

indicators.note: the non-clergy word holds the rest inside it

parts.note: lay people are those who are not clergy

indicators.note: the service letters go around the church letters

parts.note: RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A crime committed by laypeople during a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the legal term for theft, a criminal offence.

clue.text: Expel and audibly cough up with impediment?

indicators.note: audibly means the word is judged by how it is said, not how it is written

parts.note: cough up means spend; said with a stammer it comes out as s-spend

explanation.surface: A doctor's question about bringing up phlegm with a speech defect.
explanation.walkthrough: The impediment is a stammer: a stammerer saying the word for cough up (pay) repeats its first sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend a pupil is to exclude them from school for a time, which is expelling them.
